why: A routine password-manager report from a long-established domain with no link, no request and nothing urgent.
A lookalike Harborlight domain registered 18 days ago sends a macro-enabled spreadsheet and asks her to enable editing, which is a classic malware delivery.
A 17-day-old alumni lookalike domain asks her to reply with a one-time code sent to her mobile, which is an account-takeover OTP harvest.
A podcast lookalike domain created five weeks ago pushes an attachment to open and sign under a deadline, using her episode 41 appearance as the pretext.
An SMS quoting her public director ID asks her to reply with a code sent to her email, a classic OTP-relay takeover of her registry or email account.
A plain booking confirmation from a professional institute's long-established domain that asks for no action.

A claimed calendar booking leads to an external 'guest portal' that asks for her name and firm, so she should confirm the booking and the trust through her own calendar and a known contact before opening it.
A transparent founder note about a booked intro slot, on a domain whose age matches the stated company age, with no link, attachment or request beyond the meeting.
An AGM notice from the Association's long-established domain with no link or payment, only an invitation to nominate by reply or post.
A lookalike of her own firm's domain asks her to log in with her work password and confirm bank details before a cut-off, which is credential and payroll-diversion phishing.
A recruiter domain registered 24 days ago flatters her notes and pushes both an attachment and a download link, a typical malware or credential lure.
A prospective contact on a long-established domain booked through her public intro link and asks only a general question, with no link, attachment or sensitive request.
A 'Mum on a new number' WhatsApp asking for an urgent bank transfer to a third party is the classic family-impersonation scam.
A one-month-old lookalike of the Association's real domain sends a members'-area link to her personal address, which is a credential-phishing pretext.
A two-week-old lookalike Harborlight domain asks her to sign in to a 'speaker portal' with her email and steers her away from replying, which is credential phishing.
A generic webinar invitation from the long-established registry domain, with registration on that same domain and no request for codes, credentials or payment.
A regional group dinner notice from the institute's long-established domain, with payment through the group's usual page on that same domain.
A standard reschedule notification from an established scheduling service that needs no action for the original time to stand.
A routine expenses statement from an established expenses service, asking only for missing receipts, with no urgency or credential request.
An informational collection notice from a printer that asks for no payment, link or details, and says the invoice went through the firm's normal address.
A friendly heads-up from the forum's programme director that matches her genuine email and asks for nothing beyond confirming receipt.
The forum's long-established real domain shares her speaker folder on that same domain, with no credential or payment request.
A sender domain and a document-share domain registered weeks ago use her public booking link to push a pre-meeting 'shared folder', a classic credential-phishing lure.
A 12-day-old domain claims an overdue invoice for her firm's Quay offices and asks her to log in with her work email to pay under a deadline.
The supplier domain is established, but a change of bank details is the classic invoice-fraud move, so the new account must be confirmed with the supplier on a known phone number before anyone pays.
A three-week-old certificates domain targets her personal address with a download link and claims her firm's mail bounced, which is a credential or malware lure.
An 11-day-old domain claims a change of office ownership and new bank details for the licence fee, which is payment-diversion fraud.
A podcast lookalike domain registered 24 days ago asks her to set a password on a 'guest dashboard', which is credential harvesting.
